title: Sunscreen SPF50

drivers.name: Heatwave (38°C)
drivers.evidence: No direct past heatwave data, but extreme heat strongly drives sunscreen demand; 38°C is above typical summer highs in Austin; planner note confirms significance; no prior heatwave-week data, so effect is inferred from context.

drivers.name: 15% off promotion
drivers.evidence: Promotion deeper than past 10-20% off events; past 10-20% off lifts: noise-adjusted x1.02; this 15% is larger, but not unprecedented; no evidence of saturation; past 30% off lifted x1.26, but not comparable due to context.

drivers.name: Thanksgiving (holiday)
drivers.evidence: Noise-adjusted effect: x0.95 (from 2 past occurrences); effect is small and consistent with modest holiday dip; not strong enough to overcome heat and promotion.

adjustment.analysis: The baseline median is 24.8. Thanksgiving historically reduces sales (noise-adjusted x0.95), but the heatwave (38°C all week) is a strong demand driver. The 15% discount is deeper than past promotions (median 20%), and past 10-20% off events lifted sales 1.02x on average. The heatwave likely dominates the holiday dip. Past similar heat events aren't recorded, so confidence is moderate. The classical model underweights the heatwave and overweights the holiday. Adjust upward for price and weather, modestly. No double-counting.

STATISTICAL BASELINE (exponential smoothing of recent sales; it ignores events, promotions and prices):
  median 24.8 | 5%-95%: 0.0 - 66.5 | 10%-90%: 0.4 - 45.2

In the evidence below, 'vs baseline' = actual units / what this same baseline predicted for that week.
It is the multiplier that would have been right, so it maps directly onto median_multiplier.
This product's ordinary weeks already swing about +/-77% around the baseline, so a past effect smaller than that, seen only a few times, is mostly noise. The
'noise-adjusted estimate' is the effect shrunk toward x1.0 for that noise and the number of sightings.
